name: Cologne / perfume

card.summary: Alcohol-based fragrance worn for scent and impression; popular in grooming circles, with no published trials of its effect on attractiveness.
card.aka: Eau de parfum, eau de toilette, eau de cologne, fragrance
card.note: Fragrance ingredients are a known cause of contact allergy and skin irritation in some people.

quick.overview:
Perfume is a blend of aroma compounds, fixatives and a solvent, usually ethanol, worn on skin or clothing. 'Cologne' originally meant the citrus-based eau de Cologne first sold in Cologne, Germany in 1709, and in American English it now usually means a men's fragrance.
On looksmaxxing forums fragrance is treated as a low-effort add-on to grooming, with members ranking popular bottles and debating whether scent matters if the face does not. No study tests whether wearing cologne changes perceived attractiveness.
quick.mechanism: Fragrances evaporate in stages, with top notes disappearing first and base notes lasting longest. The strength of the formulation changes how long it lasts: Wikipedia lists parfum at about 15-30% aromatic compounds, eau de parfum at 15-20%, eau de toilette at 5-15% and eau de cologne at 2-3%, with brands varying [2]. The scent is smelled by others; any effect on social impressions is not established by trial data.
quick.risks: Fragrance ingredients can cause contact dermatitis, headaches or asthma symptoms in sensitive people, and patch testing with fragrance mix gives a positive reaction in about 10% of people with eczema, according to Wikipedia [3]. A 2020 review of essential oils, which are common in fragrance, also describes adverse effects including endocrine-disrupting properties for some oils [5].

lead: Perfume is a mixture of fragrant essential oils or aroma compounds, fixatives and a solvent, most often ethanol or an ethanol-water mix [2]. Cologne, in the strict sense, is eau de Cologne, a light citrus water first sold in Cologne, Germany in 1709; in American English the word now usually means any fragrance marketed to men, whatever its strength [1].

For appearance, fragrance works on the impression a person leaves at close range rather than on how they look. People wear it to smell clean and pleasant, to signal care and style, and for confidence. Laboratory studies report that a pleasant scent can raise ratings of faces and of how people see themselves and others [15][16], and that fragrance interacts with a person's own odor instead of simply covering it [14]. In looksmaxxing circles the practice has its own label, 'smellmaxxing', an offshoot of looksmaxxing in which mostly young men choose and layer fragrances, deodorants and body washes to build a signature scent [12][13].

Research on fragrance and attractiveness is small and mostly laboratory-based, with studies of body odor, perfume choice and face ratings; a 2026 systematic review of 21 studies of odors and social perception found mixed results and did not report direct effects of perfume on attractiveness [17]. Published safety research focuses on fragrance allergy and the health effects of essential oils [3][5].
infobox: Parfum/extrait, eau de parfum, eau de toilette, eau de cologne, eau fraiche [2]
Cologne about 2 hours, eau de toilette 2-4 hours, perfume up to 6-8 hours [2]
Contact allergy, skin irritation, headaches, asthma triggers [3][2]

paras: A fragrance is described by top, middle (heart) and base notes: top notes evaporate first and base notes last longest [2]. Wikipedia lists parfum or extrait at roughly 15-30% aromatic compounds, eau de parfum at 15-20% (now the most common strength), eau de toilette at 5-15% (common for men's fragrances), eau de cologne at 2-3% and eau fraiche at 3% or less [2]. The article cautions that the terms are imprecise and that a product name at different strengths can use different formulations [2]. Stronger concentrations last longer, and skin dryness, diet and medication can change how a scent performs [2].

Traditional eau de Cologne uses dilute ethanol (70-90%) as a base with citrus oils such as lemon, bergamot and neroli, and some versions add lavender, rosemary or jasmine [1]. Ingredients come from plants, from synthetic aroma compounds such as musks and, historically, from animal sources like ambergris, civet and musk, now largely replaced by synthetics [2]. Citrus essential oils are valued in perfumery and have been reviewed for biological activity and safety [21].

Fragrances are commonly grouped into families. Michael Edwards's 1983 fragrance wheel arranged them into five families, fougere, floral, oriental, woody and fresh, with subfamilies; later revisions in 2008 and 2010 changed the layout so that the main families became woody, floral, amber and fresh [10]. Retailers use such wheels to compare similar scents, though the groupings are rough and overlap [10].

Perfumery began in ancient Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Indus Valley, and a perfume maker named Tapputi appears on a second-millennium BC tablet [2]. In the 9th century Al-Kindi described many perfume recipes, and Ibn Sina (Avicenna) is credited with popularising distillation of flower oils, beginning with roses [2]. Production later spread through Islamic Spain, Italian monasteries and Hungary, and then to France, where flower cultivation for perfume grew into a major industry [2].

Giovanni Maria Farina (1685-1766), an Italian perfumer, created the fragrance in Cologne in 1709, naming it after his adopted town; in a 1708 letter to his brother he described a scent recalling an Italian spring morning [1]. It was sold to many European courts at high prices. After free trade under French control began in 1797, many firms sold products under the Eau de Cologne name, and the 4711 brand, developed by Wilhelm Mulhens, has been produced in Cologne since at least 1799 [1]. In the 18th and 19th centuries it was used as a body splash, a mild antiseptic and a remedy for fatigue and headaches [1]. In the Ottoman Empire it became a custom of hospitality, and the practice remains common in Turkey [1].

Modern perfumery began in the late 19th century with synthetic aroma chemicals such as vanillin and coumarin, and Guerlain's Jicky (1889) is cited as the first fragrance labelled a 'parfum' [2]. Most perfumers today work for large fragrance companies such as Givaudan, Firmenich, IFF, Symrise and Robertet, usually from a brief set by a fashion house or brand, and the first public perfumery school, ISIPCA, opened in 1970 [11].

Men's fragrance as a mass category grew in the 20th century. Dior introduced Eau Sauvage in 1966 as its first scent for men, composed by Edmond Roudnitska and advertised with the actor Alain Delon [22]. Old Spice began as a women's scent in 1937 from William Lightfoot Schultz's company Shulton, and a men's version followed in 1938; the brand later moved into deodorants and body sprays, and its 2010 'The Man Your Man Could Smell Like' campaign with Isaiah Mustafa won a Primetime Emmy for outstanding commercial [8]. Unilever launched Axe (Lynx in some markets) in France in 1983, and from the 1990s its advertising implied the products helped men attract women [9].

People wear cologne on skin and clothes as a finishing step after showering and dressing. Posts on T Nation show a range of habits, from a lifter who sprays cologne before training to look and smell good, to complaints about people who wear so much that it is noticeable across a gym [18][23]. A looksmax.org member described receiving compliments on cologne from strangers as part of a run of improved attention from women, in a thread about dating [19].
Storage matters for people who build collections: Wikipedia notes that perfume keeps best away from heat and light, and that sprays limit oxygen exposure compared with open bottles [2].

subs.h: What studies of scent and attractiveness report
paras: Lenochova and colleagues reported in a 2012 PLoS One paper that perfume improved perceived body odor in two experiments, but that the effect depended on the individual odor donor; in a third experiment a body odor blended with a participant's preferred perfume rated more pleasant than the same odor with a randomly assigned perfume. The authors concluded that fragrance use goes beyond masking and that people choose perfumes that blend well with their own scent [14].

A 2021 PLoS One study had women rate the self-esteem and attractiveness of men from dating-show videos while smelling sweat samples. Sweat from high-self-esteem men smelled more pleasant, but sweat alone did not change judgments of the men in video. When the sweat was masked with a fragranced body spray, the men were rated as having higher self-esteem and as more attractive [16].

A 2024 Behavioural Brain Research study recorded EEG in 22 women who rated images of other women and of themselves while smelling a commercial body wash or clean air. The pleasant fragrance raised attractiveness, confidence and femininity ratings for both self and other images and changed neural responses to faces from about 100 milliseconds [15].

Smellmaxxing is a 2020s social-media trend in which mostly young men, often teenagers, pick and layer fragrances to build a personal scent; the name borrows the '-maxxing' suffix from looksmaxxing communities, where the idea began before spreading on TikTok [12]. Creators advise lighter scents by day and richer ones in the evening, describe fragrances in wine-tasting language and share tips on application and longevity [12]. Wikipedia reports the term 'scentmaxxing' in MEL Magazine in June 2022, a Piper Sandler finding in spring 2023 of rising fragrance spending among teen boys (reported at an average of $110 a year in 2024 versus $75 in 2023), a New York Times explainer in May 2024, and coverage of growth in 'dupes' of luxury scents [12]. Mass-market names such as Axe, Impulse, Tag, RGX and Old Spice are mentioned alongside premium houses, and the Axe article links the older brand's decline to the trend [12][9].

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article describes smellmaxxing as an offshoot of looksmaxxing that emerged in the 2020s, distinct from softmaxxing practices such as skincare, grooming and exercise [13]. Side effects reported by the smellmaxxing article include school bans on fragrance and increased demand for patchouli oil, which it links to deforestation in Indonesia [12].

One member posted a ranked list of ten men's fragrances with approximate prices, from mid-range designer bottles at roughly $77-$118 to niche and luxury ones at $215-$325, and opened by saying colognes only work for people who are already good-looking [4]. Another thread has a member describing a plan to start a fragrance company [6]. In a thread asking about 'dark triad' perfume, replies said that a person who is trying to seem dark triad is not one and that the best choice is simply a scent that smells good [24].

Some body sprays and perfumes are advertised as containing human sex pheromones. Wikipedia's pheromone article states that no human pheromone has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly change behavior, that reviews describe the field as affected by small samples, publication bias and weak methods, and that candidate compounds such as androstadienone and androstenone show person- and context-dependent effects [7]. A 2026 systematic review reports inconsistent results for androstadienone and for hedione, with small effects in some studies and null results in larger ones [17].

No clinical trials have tested cologne or perfume as a treatment for appearance. Experimental psychology studies have examined fragrance and impressions in small samples of healthy adults [14][15][16], and a 2026 PRISMA systematic review of 21 laboratory studies (about 1,900 participants, mostly students) concluded that odors act as contextual cues in social judgments, with mixed results on attractiveness and no meta-analysis performed [17].

Dermatology research concerns safety: reviews of cosmetic allergy note that scented substances and preservatives are the main cause of side effects such as irritation or allergy in cosmetics [20], and a review of essential oils, which are used in cologne among many products, describes antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory and mood-related properties as well as risks including endocrine-disrupting effects for certain oils [5].

Wikipedia states that adverse reactions to fragrance can include allergic contact dermatitis, asthma attacks, headaches, nausea and allergic conjunctivitis, with contact dermatitis the most common allergic reaction [3]. Patch tests with fragrance mix give a positive result in about 10% of eczema patients, an estimated 1.7-4.1% of the general population is sensitised to fragrance mix ingredients (a figure the article marks as needing a citation), and about 2,500 fragrance ingredients are used in consumer products, of which roughly 100 are known to cause reactions in some people [3]. Products labelled 'fragrance-free' may still contain less familiar fragrance chemicals [3].

The Perfume article adds that furanocoumarins in natural extracts such as grapefruit can cause severe allergic reactions and sensitivity to ultraviolet light, that balsam of Peru is among the top five patch-test allergens and has been barred as a fragrance compound by the International Fragrance Association (IFRA) since 1982, and that some synthetic musks have been reviewed by EU safety committees and the US EPA, which found no human health concern [2]. Since 11 March 2005 the EU has required labelling of 26 recognised fragrance allergens above set thresholds, which led to reformulation of oakmoss-based chypre and fougere styles [2]. In the US, companies rarely disclose full ingredient lists, citing trade secrets [2].

Aerosol body sprays carry their own cautions: a Wikipedia account records a 2008 death of a 12-year-old boy in Derbyshire, England after heavy use of Lynx in a confined space, which a coroner linked to heart failure, and notes injuries from fire stunts with Axe spray and Unilever's warnings that the product is flammable [9].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org fragrance is a side topic: members post ranked lists of popular bottles and frame scent as an add-on to appearance rather than a replacement for it [4]. The wider smellmaxxing trend on TikTok treats scent as a layered, personal signature [12].

claims.claim: Cologne only works if you are already good-looking.
claims.believers: The author of a looksmax.org cologne guide opens with the statement that colognes only work for people who are already 'GL' (good-looking), then lists ten popular bottles with prices [4].
claims.experts: No published study has tested whether the effect of fragrance depends on the wearer's looks. In a 2021 experiment a fragranced body spray raised ratings of men's attractiveness in videos [16].

claims.claim: A good fragrance makes people see you as more attractive.
claims.believers: Smellmaxxing creators and forum members describe fragrance as a way to leave a better impression and report compliments [12][19].
claims.experts: A 2024 EEG study in 22 women found a pleasant scent raised attractiveness and confidence ratings of faces, and a 2021 study found body-spray-masked sweat led to higher attractiveness ratings; a 2026 review found mixed effects overall and did not report direct perfume effects on attractiveness [15][16][17].

claims.believers: Many wearers describe cologne as a way to mask sweat and smell fresh; this is the everyday rationale for deodorant-style body sprays.
claims.experts: Lenochova and colleagues report that perfume interacts with an individual's own odor, with people preferring blends of their own odor with their favourite perfume [14]; a conditioning study cited in the 2026 review found people could still tell apart individuals wearing the same fragrance [17].

claims.claim: Pheromone colognes make you sexually attractive.
claims.believers: Some products are marketed as containing human sex pheromones that act as aphrodisiacs [7].
claims.experts: Wikipedia states that no such claim has been demonstrated in peer-reviewed research, and a 2026 review calls the evidence for androstadienone and hedione inconsistent [7][17].

claims.claim: A more expensive or niche bottle gives a better impression than a cheap one.
claims.believers: Looksmax.org rankings list niche and luxury bottles among the 'best of the best', and smellmaxxing coverage notes a shift from cheap sprays to premium brands [4][12].
claims.experts: No published study has compared perceived attractiveness across price tiers.

claims.claim: Different scents suit different occasions, lighter by day and richer at night.
claims.believers: TikTok smellmaxxing creators give this as a standard rule [12].
claims.experts: This is a convention of perfumery and retail advice; no study has tested it. Wikipedia notes stronger concentrations last longer [2].

claims.believers: T Nation posters complain that strong cologne is noticeable across a gym [18].
claims.experts: Reviews list headaches, asthma attacks and skin reactions among reported responses to fragrance [3].

claims.claim: Fragrance can cause allergic reactions in some wearers.
claims.believers: In two US surveys summarised by Wikipedia, about 30.5% of people said that scented products worn by others irritated them [3].
claims.experts: Patch testing finds about 10% of eczema patients react to fragrance mix, and the EU requires labelling of 26 allergens [3][2].

angle.text: Cologne adds a scent layer to grooming. In small laboratory studies a pleasant fragrance raised attractiveness and confidence ratings and shaped impressions of men whose sweat was masked with body spray [15][16]. The effect lasts for the hours the scent lasts [2].
